Article Title: Rejected a job offer for chess, now India's 100th Grandmaster: How Anuj Shrivatri became Madhya Pradesh's first GM
Article Text:
Anuj Shrivatri is India's 100th GM

A father's hobby, a son's career

MP's top chess players in Anuj Shrivatri, now a GM, IM Akshat Khamparia, and IM Ayush Sharma (Special Arrangements)

The price of chasing the dream

Becoming a Grandmaster despite losing in Round 1

Anuj Shrivatri's performance at the 7th ASEAN Plus Individual Open Chess Championship

'Satisfied isn't really the right word'

A banner with faces of prominent chess players in MP (Special Arrangements)

NEW DELHI: While India was preparing to light diyas for Diwali, Anuj Shrivatri was about 2,800 miles away, in a tournament hall in the Philippines, closing out a game that would make him the country's 100th Grandmaster and the first his state, Madhya Pradesh, had ever produced.Before this Sunday, India had 99 Grandmasters, and Madhya Pradesh had none. The tally has now gone up by one, thanks to a 22-year-old from Katni who rejected a corporate job offer to chase this exact moment.As he prepares to board a flight back home, his latest challenge is to contain the euphoria felt in his voice."The feeling right now is mostly relief," Anuj told TimesofIndia.com from the Philippines, barely a day after winning the 7th ASEAN Plus Individual Open Chess Championship and securing the GM title directly."I had been trying for the GM title for a long time. There were so many times my GM norms were missed. At least four or five times I was really close, and it slipped away. So now that the title is finally complete, I'm feeling a lot of relief."Shrivatri's parents, Ashok Kumar Shrivatri, a teacher with the railways, and Manorama Shrivatri, a teacher at a government school, had lived through every one of those near misses alongside him, making this ve occasion all the more special."They're very happy. They also know I'd been struggling with this for a long time. I was playing well, but sometimes the results just weren't coming. Now that the title is finally complete, they're very happy. And since it happened during Diwali, it's an even bigger joy for them," he added with a smile.Chess entered Shrivatri's life through a parent's old college pastime."My father used to play chess during his college days," he recalled. "He was quite fond of the game, so when I was young, around five or six, he introduced me to it. Then both my elder brother and I took a liking to it."His brother eventually drifted away from the board; he now works as a software engineer in Bengaluru. Shrivatri didn't.A succession of coaches shaped him from there. Virendra Tiwari, who taught him his very first moves, then Nikhilesh Jain, then Yashpal Arora, and finally Rajesh Bahadur, under whose guidance Shrivatri became an International Master (IM) in 2019.After that, he says, it was mostly self-directed work, punctuated by sessions with respected Grandmasters such as Vishnu Prasanna, Swayams Mishra and Swapnil Dhopade whenever he needed outside eyes on his game.What followed the IM title, though, wasn't a straight climb."After 2019, I was very motivated, but then Covid came," he continued. "After that, I wasn't sure whether to pursue chess as a career or focus on my studies. At that point, chess didn't feel certain enough, and I wasn't sure of myself either, so I decided to focus on studies."He completed his BTech degree in Computer Science at Lovely Professional University, and it was only in 2025, playing tournaments on the side, almost as an afterthought, that something shifted."I felt a change in my play, in my temperament. I thought, no, I should give chess a real shot, give it a year or two and try to become a GM," he recalled.The timing forced a genuine choice. His college internship ended just as a full-time job offer from the company landed in his inbox."I was fairly certain by then that completing the GM title would be a great thing," he revealed. "So I quit the company and went full-time into chess."The decision to go full-time in chess came with its challenges. With no sponsorship, every trip abroad came out of his own pocket, financed in large part by what he earned playing rapid tournaments and coaching gigs."Finances were the biggest struggle, because I was managing everything myself and there was no sponsorship as such. I was earning money from rapid tournaments and spending it on trips abroad," he admitted.That math also explains why getting an opportunity to play against elite, 2600-plus-rated opposition has been difficult."The strong players are usually found in very niche tournaments, a big event in Kazakhstan, or a strong open in Qatar. But going there is financially a very risky decision. One tournament can cost around a lakh rupees just to go and play," he added.In the Philippines, Shrivatri lost his opening-round game. He feels what went wrong was his decision to play aggressively as Black."I took on too much risk, and my position became very uncomfortable. I think it was simply the fault of my opening," he recalled.He rebuilt from there with a complete change of approach."For the rest of the games, I played very solid with Black. I told myself I'd try to create chances, but if it didn't work out and my opponent played well, it was fine to take the draw. That approach helped me a lot, because at some point or another, people make mistakes. You just have to wait for them."What followed was an unbeaten run in his remaining eight games, with six wins and two draws. He finished the tournament with 7/9, half a point ahead of second-placed Vietnamese GM Nguyen Duc Hoa.Hailing from the same city, Akshat Khamparia, the state’s first IM, recalls a boy who was reserved away from the board but unusually mature on it.Even as a youngster, he leaned on patience and structure rather than fireworks, picking apart positions move by careful move long before he had the rating to back that style up.Khamparia, MP Chess's committee convener who has spent years building up its tournament circuit, has made a habit of promoting the state's young players at every event he runs, with banners with their faces up at venues."We've done a lot for Anuj too," Khamparia said. "We've highlighted him everywhere, in events, at every opportunity we get."It's the same persistence that, separately, saw Khamparia spend years nudging Shrivatri toward the career security of a sports-quota job with Indian Railways.And after years of him pushing Anuj, the process has now gone through. Anuj’s medical has been completed, and his joining Western Railway is in its final stages.Even now, Shrivatri resists calling himself satisfied."Satisfied isn't really the right word," he said, "because I have a pretty strong opinion that you should never become complacent in life. You should enjoy the milestone, of course, but in general, you should never settle. That's something I try to follow."So, what is next for him? The 22-year-old concluded, "There are two things I'm sure about. I want to cross a 2600 rating, and I want to win as many tournaments as I can. Those are my two goals in chess right now."
Article Summary: Anuj Shrivatri is India's 100th Grandmaster and the first from Madhya Pradesh. The 22-year-old from Katni rejected a corporate job offer to chase this exact moment. He won the 7th ASEAN Plus Individual Open Chess Championship in the Philippines.

Article Title: 'Khawaja is 100% accurate': David Warner backs former teammate, questions Sandpapergate investigation
Article Text:
Usman Khawaja and David Warner. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

Warner questions investigation, says Khawaja was not interviewed

What Khawaja said about Sandpaper Gate

Khawaja defends his remarks: 'I haven't thrown anyone under the bus'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Australia opener David Warner has thrown his weight behind Usman Khawaja amid the renewed controversy surrounding the 2018 Sandpaper Gate scandal, insisting that his former teammate's revelations are accurate and that the truth about one of Australian cricket's darkest episodes needed to come out.Warner, who was among the three players punished by Cricket Australia (CA) following the ball-tampering scandal in South Africa, expressed his full support for Khawaja in a video posted on Instagram. He also questioned the credibility of the investigation conducted after the incident, pointing out that Khawaja, despite being present alongside Cameron Bancroft, was never interviewed."It's been eight years since I've spoken on this topic. And Uzzie (Usman Khawaja), I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth. It's out there. People wanted to know it; you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' Talking about selling a book—this is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes," Warner said.His intervention comes after excerpts from Khawaja's forthcoming autobiography, Sabr, reignited debate over the events of the 2018 Test series against South Africa.Khawaja has claimed that knowledge of the ball-tampering operation extended beyond the three players who were formally punished, and that the responsibility should have been accepted collectively by the team.Warner's strongest criticism was directed at the process followed by CA after the Cape Town Test, where Bancroft was caught on camera using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball.According to Warner, the investigation was rushed and incomplete, particularly because Khawaja, who was sitting next to Bancroft, was not questioned."Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched. Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft; Uzzie was not interviewed. How is that a thorough investigation? It baffles me. We're not here to point fingers, and we're not opening our wounds. It's about accountability, transparency, ensuring that the truth is properly examined. And perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability and start asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it," Warner said.Warner also spoke about the personal toll the scandal had taken on his family. He revealed that he had recently been forced to explain the events to his daughters, particularly his 12-year-old Ivy, who wanted to understand the images of the family being surrounded by cameras and the emotional scenes that followed the scandal."Now, there were a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people, and there were a lot of people who stayed silent. The last couple of days, I've had to be—I've been talking to my daughters, and that's why it's taken me a couple of days to get this out, because I've had to tell them exactly what had happened. Especially my 12-year-old, Ivy, wanting to know why we were holding her, why there were so many cameras, why we were crying on TV," he said.Describing the conversation as difficult, Warner said he had emphasised the importance of telling the truth."That was a hard thing to do. But one thing I did say is, 'Girls, tell the truth, because lies will eventually get out.' It was a very tough time. This is for everyone in Australia. It's been—it's been the question that everyone's been asking. Uzzie, you've said it how it is. It's 100% accurate," he added."It's been a tough time for my family, Steve and Cameron no doubt, but this is what needed to come out. I fully support that, Uzzie," Warner concluded.The controversy resurfaced after excerpts from Khawaja's autobiography, reported by the Sydney Morning Herald, claimed that the ball-tampering episode was not limited to the Cape Town Test and that the team had also used sandpaper during the preceding Test in Port Elizabeth.Khawaja's account challenged the long-standing position that only Warner, then captain Steve Smith and Bancroft had prior knowledge of the plan. In an interview ahead of the book's release, he said: "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."He also recalled pushing for collective responsibility in the dressing room after the Cape Town incident, arguing that the team should stand together rather than leave three players to carry the consequences.Khawaja's account further revealed a disagreement over that proposal. He claimed two teammates opposed his suggestion that the entire group accept responsibility."This was the most disappointing thing for me. I knew who those two guys were, and it was ludicrous; out of everyone, it was them. It showed me their true colours, though. When the going got tough, all they cared about was themselves. But I was not going to stop fighting this cause," Khawaja wrote.Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann rejected aspects of Khawaja's claims, while the controversy also drew criticism from former England captain Michael Vaughan. The Australian bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon had previously denied knowing about the ball-tampering plan before Bancroft was shown on the stadium screen.With the revelations triggering a backlash, Khawaja took to social media to clarify what he meant by saying the entire team was responsible. He insisted that his reference to "all of us" was about collective accountability and not an attempt to accuse individual teammates."Alright, it’s time to clear up some facts because the media has taken this to the moon, as expected."I stayed quiet yesterday, but number one, if you read my article, you would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us that’s implying that, whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened. Together, as a team, we need to take that collectively. That is all," he said.However, Khawaja did not withdraw his assertion that the wider group knew about the episode."But now that everyone’s talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah. I won’t deny that either."But I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book. Contrary to all the headlines the clickbait media would have you think. Don’t get caught up in this s***."He also rejected suggestions that he had waited eight years to reveal the details simply to generate publicity for his autobiography. Khawaja said he had deliberately held back the account until the Australian team had returned from South Africa and had even spoken to Cummins before deciding when to make it public."What I say now isn’t a reflection of them anymore, and now my words don’t influence the team at all. I speak for myself. But even so, I refused to publish any of this while the boys were still in South Africa. That’s why I called Pat (Cummins)."Why would someone who really wants to increase the sale of his book refuse the greatest marketing opportunity he has? I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus... those three guys [Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft] who took the blame for all of us, they’re the victims," he said.Under CA's findings at the time, Smith and Warner received 12-month bans from international and domestic cricket, while Bancroft was suspended for nine months.
Article Summary: Former Australia opener David Warner has thrown his weight behind Usman Khawaja. Warner says it's time for the truth to come out about the ball-tampering scandal. He also questioned the credibility of the investigation conducted after the incident. Warner also spoke about the personal toll the scandal had taken on his family.

HAMILTON: The Indian cricket team is firming up its preparations for the upcoming two-match Test series against New Zealand. The players in the squad will leave for Wellington from Hamilton and will be assisted by batting coach Sitanshu Kotak and bowling coach Morne Morkel . The players in the India A set-up, in Christchurch, will link up with the group in Wellington.Kotak revealed on Monday that the team management is also considering keeping Arshdeep Singh, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi back for the Test camp, and head coach Gautam Gambhir will soon make the final call. The head coach himself will stay back with the ODI team."Gautam will have to be here, One Day World Cup is coming, so he will be staying here, and probably Sairaj (Bahutule) will stay here. Me, Morne (Morkel) and some other staff will go to Wellington, this is the plan. It will be finalised by Gautam, so it can change. We will just try and see that their (Test squad) loading, their fitness, their practice, they should do enough preparation, as much as the conditions permit us. Arsh (Arshdeep Singh), (Auqib) Nabi, and Gurnoor (Brar), if I am not wrong, will stay back for Tests," said Kotak on Monday.India played the first two ODIs in challenging conditions and Kotak felt while the colour of the ball will change, the experience will hold the Test-bound players in good stead for the two-match series.Both Auckland and Wellington fixtures were low-scoring affairs and batters from both teams found life difficult in conditions which were seaming and swinging, and offered encouraging bounce to the bowlers. With a short turnaround time between the ODI and Test series, the Indian camp is hoping that the Wellington sessions will keep the squad ready for Basin Reserve opener.Additionally, players like Jasprit Bumrah, Ravindra Jadeja, Devdutt Padikkal, Akash Deep, Sai Sudharsan have been with the India A team and got some crucial game time under their belt."The wicket in both the ODIs had swing and when it stopped after 4-6 overs, there was seam movement and a little awkward bounce also. So, in hindsight, it is a good thing, because in the Test match, the same thing can happen... only the ball will be red. Yes, the intent and mindset will be of One Day in One Day, but one thing is that with the wickets here, thicker grass, 12-14 [mm of grass, and the conditions, you can get an idea.Even if there is more green in the Test pitch, there is not much green in this one. But it is quite a good condition to play... it is challenging."Plus, there are many India A matches which the red ball players are playing. So that is also a big advantage for batters and bowlers because they would know where to bowl, what length to bowl, how much to hit, how much to release, and what help to expect."So all in all, the preparation has been very good and on top of that, the Test players are going for a camp on the 11th, so we will also get 5-6 sessions. Fingers crossed, we should be ready for the Test series as well," explained Kotak.After wrapping up their ODI committments, Shubman Gill and other members of the Test squad will head to Wellington while the remaining team heads to Tauranga for the last two fixtures, where the team will be led by Shreyas Iyer.
Article Summary: The Indian cricket team is firming up its preparations for the upcoming two- match Test series against New Zealand. The players in the squad will leave for Wellington from Hamilton and will be assisted by batting coach Sitanshu Kotak and bowling coach Morne Morkel. Kotak revealed on Monday that the team management is also considering keeping Arshdeep Singh, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi back.

Article Title: ‘Coaches are afraid’: Ex-India coach opens up on confronting Virat Kohli over technical flaw
Article Text:
Virat Kohli

Former India assistant coach Ryan ten Doeschate has opened up about a behind-the-scenes conversation with Virat Kohli during India's tour of Australia, revealing how carefully he planned a technical intervention with the batting superstar after noticing a recurring flaw in his batting. Kohli had endured a difficult run during the tour, repeatedly getting dismissed while attempting to drive deliveries outside the off stump. With the same mode of dismissal becoming a talking point, questions were raised about whether the Indian coaching staff was doing enough to address the issue.Speaking on the talkSPORT Cricket podcast, Ten Doeschate explained that approaching an established international star with technical suggestions is not always straightforward. He believes the growing influence of players in modern cricket has made several coaches hesitant about intervening when senior players are going through a difficult phase."I think a lot of coaches are afraid to make interventions because it can be seen that you are, you know, trying to justify your job, or you're interfering, or just saying things for the sake of saying it," Ten Doeschate said."You've got to strike the balance of making an intervention that's going to help the player, or confusing them."The former Netherlands all-rounder said he was determined not to let the fear of how a player might react prevent him from offering advice. He recalled eventually approaching Kohli during the fourth Test of the Australia tour to discuss his repeated dismissals."I never want to be a coach who is scared of an opinion of someone else for stepping in, for saying the right thing. I actually was just telling a really great story about Virat and the troubles he had in Australia with driving the ball and nicking off. Eventually, in the fourth Test, I went to intervene and chat to him. And he was brilliant about it! And he actually wanted someone to chat to him," he said.However, Ten Doeschate admitted that initiating such a conversation with a player of Kohli's stature can be a delicate exercise. According to him, coaches need to consider not just what they want to communicate but also how and when they deliver the message."But my sense is, for a coach to go to a player like Virat Kohli and intervene and almost call them out on what's happening can be dangerous for you as a coach. And I think getting the wording right around that and how you deliver it is so important."The way the power shift has moved towards the players in the modern era does mean that a lot of coaches are scared to bring up topics or at least get talking about it."Ten Doeschate further explained that the objective of coaching should not necessarily be to convince a player to abandon his preferred approach. Instead, it should involve understanding the batter's thinking and finding ways to make adjustments without taking away what works for him.He recalled how Kohli explained his reasoning behind continuing to play the drive in the manner he did, making the exchange a discussion rather than a one-sided technical instruction."You don't have to agree. You might say, 'I want to drive on the up for these reasons,' and that's actually what happened with Virat. He really explained why he wanted to play in the way he played, and then you can tweak around that," Ten Doeschate revealed.The former assistant coach also highlighted the danger of introducing technical doubts into a batter's mind at the wrong moment. A player preparing to face a high-quality fast bowler could become distracted if he starts thinking too much about a particular aspect of his technique."There's always a risk that you sort of unsettle his frame of mind. You know, he might be in a really good place, and now you say, 'You know, I've noticed when you're pulling... you're just taking your eye off the ball.' Technically, you might want him to watch the ball a little bit longer, but now all of a sudden he's thinking about pulling, and he's got to go out and face Mitchell Starc . So that's not the time to do it," he said.Ten Doeschate revealed that the conversation with Kohli had been on his mind for some time before he eventually found an appropriate opportunity during a rain interruption.He said the repeated nature of Kohli's dismissals had prompted him to think carefully about how to raise the subject without making the batter feel that his technique was being questioned."In that situation, it had been bubbling away, and it was more a case of me building up the courage and delivering it in the right way. I was lucky enough to have a decent relationship with Virat. He's obviously not someone who needs a lot of coaching, and that was one thing that really stuck out-the manner of the dismissal being so same-same," he said.Explaining how he eventually approached the conversation, Ten Doeschate said he deliberately avoided making it sound like a direct criticism of Kohli's batting."So I had thought about it a lot, and I thought how I could deliver it. You know, I'm not going to go to him and say, 'Mate, you've got cover drives all over the show.' But I then worked out a time-it was during a rain break-where I could deliver it in quite a non-confrontational way. And credit to him, the way he took it on ended up being a really great discussion."While the intervention did not produce the desired outcome towards the end of the series, Ten Doeschate considered the experience an important lesson in communication and coaching."Unfortunately, it didn't deliver the results we wanted towards the back end of the series, but you know, I'd say if you can deliver it to someone like him, you can deliver it to anyone. Just finding the right way of dropping your message is really important," he added.
Article Summary: Former India assistant coach Ryan ten Doeschate has opened up about a behind- the-scenes conversation with Virat Kohli during India's tour of Australia. He revealed how carefully he planned a technical intervention with the batting superstar after noticing a recurring flaw in his batting. Kohli had endured a difficult run, repeatedly getting dismissed while attempting to drive deliveries outside the off stump.

Article Title: Mushfiqur Rahim makes Bangladesh cricket history, becomes first to score 7,000 Test runs
Article Text:
Mushfiqur Rahim (PTI Photo)

From 5,000 to 7,000: Mushfiqur's remarkable journey

Bangladesh's most experienced Test cricketer

Bangladesh veteran Mushfiqur Rahim added another landmark to his illustrious career, becoming the first batter from the country to score 7,000 runs in Test cricket. The 39-year-old achieved the milestone in the ongoing second Test against West Indies in Sylhet, further cementing his place among Bangladesh's greatest players in the longest format.Mushfiqur reached the landmark when he took a single off West Indies spinner Roston Chase to move to nine runs in his innings. The veteran initially appeared unaware of the achievement, but acknowledged the moment after his teammates rose from their seats in the dressing room to applaud him.The milestone was another reward for Mushfiqur's remarkable longevity and consistency in Test cricket. He had missed the opening Test of the series because of a finger injury but returned for the second match to add another chapter to his career.Mushfiqur had already established himself as Bangladesh's leading Test run-scorer when he became the country's first batter to reach 5,000 runs in 2022 and 6,000 in 2024. He has now taken that record to another level, becoming the first Bangladesh player to breach the 7,000-run mark.He has accumulated 7,000 runs in his 107th Test, having needed only 25 innings to progress from 6,000 to 7,000. His tally includes 14 centuries, with his highest score being an unbeaten 219.Mominul Haque is second on Bangladesh's all-time Test run-scoring list with 5,293 runs, while former opener Tamim Iqbal is third. Mominul has scored 13 Test centuries, while Tamim has registered 10.Mushfiqur's latest achievement comes in a match in which his record for the highest individual score by a Bangladesh batter in Tests was surpassed. Towhid Hridoy struck an unbeaten 242 earlier in the ongoing Sylhet Test, going past Mushfiqur's previous best of 219 not out.Having made his international debut in 2005, Mushfiqur is Bangladesh's most experienced Test cricketer. He became the first player from the country to feature in 100 Tests in November 2025 and is now appearing in his 107th match.His journey in the format has been one of steady evolution. Initially a lower-middle-order batter and wicketkeeper, Mushfiqur took 20 Tests to reach his first 1,000 runs. His batting responsibilities grew as he became a more established member of the side, particularly after taking over as Bangladesh captain in 2011.Over the years, he developed into one of the team's most dependable batters, producing crucial runs across conditions and against different opponents. His ability to maintain consistency over such a long career has been reflected in the latest milestone.Mushfiqur has also made significant contributions in limited-overs cricket, scoring 6,697 runs in ODIs and 1,495 in T20 Internationals. He has since retired from both formats, with Test cricket remaining the stage on which he continues to extend his legacy.
Article Summary: Mushfiqur Rahim becomes first Bangladesh player to score 7,000 runs in Test cricket. The 39-year-old reached the milestone in the ongoing second Test against West Indies in Sylhet. The milestone was another reward for his remarkable longevity and consistency. He became the first player from Bangladesh to feature in 100 Tests in November 2025.

Article Title: 'Stay calm': New Zealand coach impressed by India's young pacers, tells batters to adapt to tough pitches
Article Text:
Ronchi impressed by India's young pace attack

'Stay calm': Ronchi's advice to batters

NEW DELHI: New Zealand batting coach Luke Ronchi has been impressed by India's inexperienced pace attack, which has repeatedly troubled the home batters in the ongoing ODI series, but believes the key to surviving on challenging surfaces is adaptability rather than an obsession with scoring rates.India's quartet of Arshdeep Singh , Auqib Nabi, Anshul Kamboj and Gurnoor Brar have accounted for 17 of New Zealand's 20 wickets across the first two ODIs, with the hosts being bowled out for 185 and 134 respectively.With the third ODI approaching, Ronchi praised the young Indian bowlers for their ability to adjust their lengths and lines to conditions that have offered assistance to fast bowlers."Yeah, they've been really good. They're asking questions of batters and it'll be quite cool for them. They're going into games where the ball isn't flying around, the ball is actually assisting them and then they'll be happy with that," the former New Zealand wicketkeeper-batter said.Ronchi was particularly impressed by how India's young fast bowlers have adapted to conditions after spending considerable time bowling on flatter subcontinental pitches."They are so used to bowling on flat wickets, it's realising what is the right length, what's the right line, the ball is swinging a bit (and) how do we bowl the way we want to bowl to make it hard for the batters.""They've done that really well and they've challenged our batters and taken wickets early and made different impacts in different games, so it's exciting to see when you see younger guys come into the game and perform and try and push their case to be playing more and more and more," he added.The bowling-friendly conditions have also provided both teams with valuable preparation ahead of the two-Test series beginning November 19."Technically, yeah, they will (prepare better) because that's traditionally what we have here for Test cricket, it's a lot greener surfaces," Ronchi said. "In reality, that Wellington surface was more of a Test type of surface, so it's grasping hold of that and realising that, and it will help both teams."Ronchi believes batters need to understand that challenging pitches demand a different approach and that scoring rates cannot always remain the priority."At the moment, it's quite cool; the bowlers have actually got the upper hand, so there's nothing wrong with that. Traditionally, you go around the world, especially in India if teams don't make 400 you're in trouble, so it's just ridiculous."He added that bowlers deserve assistance from conditions and that both sides have made good use of it."The other night, if either team had made 200 batting first, that would have been a massive score, so it's realising that okay, for 10 overs you might be going at two, three (runs) an over, you're actually still going okay."Ronchi stressed that staying composed and assessing conditions was crucial, particularly with pitches likely to vary across venues."It's just trying to stay calm and realise the adaptability of what you need to do in those moments, but they're always continuing conversations because again, tomorrow it might be an amazing wicket and then again, we go to Mount Maunganui, it's a different wicket again," he said.
Article Summary: New Zealand batting coach Luke Ronchi has been impressed by India's young pace attack. India's quartet of Arshdeep Singh, Auqib Nabi, Anshul Kamboj and Gurnoor Brar have accounted for 17 of New Zealand's 20 wickets across the first two ODIs. Ronchi praised the young Indian bowlers for their ability to adjust their lengths and lines to conditions.

Oaminal Cup in the Philippines on Sunday.The 22-year-old from Katni, ranked India No. 76, secured the title through a special format that awarded a direct GM title to the winner, bypassing the usual requirement of three norms across 27 games and an Elo rating of 2500. His peak rating was 2483, achieved in June.Fourth seed Anuj, rated 2450, lost to home player Arca Karlo in the opening round but recovered strongly, winning six of his next eight games to finish with seven points. He finished half a point ahead of Vietnam GM Nguyen Duc Hoa and pocketed $3,000. The format meant Anuj faced only two players from the top 10 seeds and none rated higher than him. He finished with a performance rating of 2586, short of the 2600 required for a conventional GM norm, and is expected to gain around 15 rating points.Several Indian players, including Ayush Sharma, Neelash Saha, Nitish Belurkar, Mohd Imran and Ajay Parvathareddy, appeared better placed to become the country’s 100th GM, having already met either the norm or rating requirement.However, Anuj seized the opportunity to enter the record books.An International Master since 2019, Anuj becomes the latest Indian to earn the GM title through a special Fide-approved event. Divya Deshmukh, too, became India's fourth female GM through the Women's World Cup rather than the conventional route.India is not the first country to reach 100 grandmasters. Russia, the US, Ukraine and Germany have already crossed the milestone, with Russia boasting more than 250. More than 2,000 players have been awarded the GM title worldwide.The ASEAN Plus tournament was eligible to award a direct GM title provided at least four GMs and six IMs competed in every round. Although India is not part of the 11-member ASEAN chess bloc, Indian players were allowed to participate.
Article Summary: Anuj Shrivatri becomes India's 100th chess grandmaster. He won the 7th ASEAN Plus Individual Open Chess Championship Governor Henry S. Oaminal Cup in the Philippines on Sunday. The 22-year-old from Katni secured the title through a special format that awarded a direct GM title.

NEW DELHI: World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen and 23 other players are set to take over the board at the Total Chess World Championship Tour pilot in Budapest, but the build-up to the event has been shadowed by questions about its format.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, Total Chess World Championship chief Kjell Madland defended the pilot’s format, under which qualification for the semi-finals is decided purely by fast classical. Rapid and Blitz come into play only after the group stage, which means 20 of the 24 players will not play either format before they are out of the race for the title.The tournament begins on November 10 at the Anantara New York Palace in Budapest, Hungary. A nine-round Swiss-system blitz tournament and the opening ceremony are held on the same day.Next up, the 24 players are then split into four groups of six, with the four highest-rated players in separate groups. Each group plays a double round robin at fast classical, which gives 45 minutes per player and a 30-second increment from move one, with three points for a win and one for a draw.The four group winners go through to the semi-finals, where they play Rapid and Blitz as well as fast classical.The other 20 players will play for positions 5 to 24 in all three formats, but they will not be in the race for the finale, which will take place on November 20.Madland, the founder and CEO of Norway Chess and the Total Chess World Championship Tour, rejected the suggestion that those 20 players are sidelined.“They are not eliminated,” he told this website. “All the players will play all the games until the last day.”The nine-round Blitz Swiss does not count towards qualification, but its standings break ties in the group tables. “If players are tied in the group stage, then we will look at the results in the blitz tournament to decide who is number two, three and four,” Madland added.He said the group stage uses fast classical because the time control, announced by FIDE in September 2025, is relatively new, and this is the best way to test it.“Since fast classical is a new format, it’s also good to have attention on this, so we think this is a good way to do it,” he said. “After that, the number one in all the groups will fight for first place, the number two will fight for the next place, and so on. But all the players will play all the games.”The knockouts use a different structure. The semi-finals, the third-place match and the final are each played over two days. Every day has four Blitz games, then two Rapid games, then one fast classical game, and scores reset each day. If the two days are split or both level, an Armageddon game decides the match. White gets ten minutes with no increment, and Black gets seven minutes with a one-second increment from move 41. A draw, in this case, wins the match for Black.Madland accepted that the format will draw questions. “Of course, we need to find a good way to do it. This is what we have done, and the players like it,” he noted. “Hopefully it will be good, but there will always be some questions about this and that. Hopefully this will work well.”He said the pilot status leaves room to adjust, though not drastically.“We don’t think we will do big adjustments. Hopefully we don’t need to think about that,” he said. “But when we have the pilot, it’s of course much easier if something is needed with rules and regulations. That’s possible. This is of course the reason we have this pilot, to test everything.”The pilot is the opening event of the Total Chess World Championship Tour 2026–27, which offers two places in the 2028 Candidates Tournament. It was announced by Norway Chess in October 2025, is endorsed by FIDE, and is co-organised with the Hungarian Chess Federation.Madland said the response so far has been positive.“We have received a lot of good feedback from everywhere, from players, from media and from fans,” he said. “People are very open to this, and I feel that people have also waited for something like this, because combining all the formats is a way to find the best players.”On why the format was built this way, he said: “I had a feeling for some years that we should build something that included everything, because we have talked with players, fans, media and everything.” He added that it would help the sport grow “in the media, in OTT and TV channels, in media deals.”“I hope people find this very interesting, and also that they are open to seeing that chess needs to change a bit to meet the new audience, so there will be more interest in it,” he said.
Article Summary: The tournament begins on November 10 at the Anantara New York Palace in Budapest, Hungary. A nine-round Swiss-system blitz tournament and the opening ceremony are held on the same day. The 24 players are then split into four groups of six, with the four highest-rated players in separate groups. Each group plays a double round robin at fast classical, which gives 45 minutes per player.

Article Title: Shourya Ambure wins historic bronze, India's first track and field medal at Dakar Youth Olympics

NEW DELHI: India's Shourya Ambure produced a memorable performance at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, winning a historic bronze medal in the women's 100m hurdles to deliver the country's first track and field medal at the ongoing edition on Sunday.The 17-year-old from Maharashtra clocked a personal best of 13.59 seconds to finish third in the final, narrowly missing out on the silver medal by just 0.02 seconds. China's Zhang Keyi clinched gold with a timing of 13.17 seconds, while France's Anna Peeters took silver in 13.57 seconds.Ambure's achievement was particularly significant as she was India's only track and field athlete competing at the Games. She also bettered her personal best twice on the same day, underlining her consistency and ability to deliver on the big occasion.Ambure had already set the tone in the semi-finals, clocking 13.77 seconds to qualify for the medal race. She then raised her performance in the final, shaving 0.18 seconds off that mark to secure a place on the podium.The Maharashtra sprinter's bronze adds another significant chapter to her growing career. In the space of just 18 months, she has won medals at the Asian U18 Championships, Asian Youth Games and Youth Olympic Games, establishing herself as one of India's promising young hurdlers.Her performance also provided a significant boost to India's athletics campaign in Dakar, with the youngster making the most of her opportunity as the country's sole representative in track and field.Ambure's bronze was India's eighth medal at the Dakar Youth Olympics, taking the country's tally to three silver and five bronze medals.Earlier, wrestler Taniya had secured India's first-ever beach wrestling medal at the Games, winning silver in the women's 75kg category. She lost 1-2 to China's Min Zhao, the 2025 U17 world champion in the 69kg category, in the gold medal bout. Taniya had defeated USA's Matilda Hruby 3-1 in the semi-finals.Other silver medallists for India include Khushbu Rajakbhai Darjada in women's 63kg judo and Tanvi Patri in badminton.Swimming also contributed three medals, with Dhinidhi Desinghu winning bronze in the women's 100m and 200m freestyle events, while Tirthank Pegu claimed bronze in the men's 200m butterfly. Desinghu became the first Indian to win multiple medals at a single Youth Olympics edition, while Pegu secured India's first-ever male swimming medal at the Games.Rajkumari Lanchenbi Chanu added another bronze in the women's changquan combined wushu event.
Article Summary: Shourya Ambure wins bronze in women's 100m hurdles at Dakar 2026 Games. The 17-year-old clocked a personal best of 13.59 seconds to finish third. China's Zhang Keyi clinched gold, while France's Anna Peeters took silver. India's medal tally reaches eight with three silver and five bronze medals.

Article Title: Wanted: Role clarity for KL Rahul
Article Text:
KL Rahul (AP Photo)

There have been copious amounts of chatter on social media and many column inches devoted in newspapers discussing how the ODIs in New Zealand could act as a dress rehearsal for the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.Many feel the conditions in New Zealand mirror those that India may encounter in southern Africa this time next year. Judging by the bounce and movement that one saw in Auckland and Wellington in the first two ODIs, the argument may not be too far away from the truth. The Indian team management, though, may have stumbled upon an uncomfortable truth.Their best No. 5 batter features in the XI, but he is not batting there.For far too long in his 12-year international career, KL Rahul has been seen as Indian cricket’s utility man. Someone who can fill gaps rather than command a role. He has opened, batted in the middle order, kept wickets, played as a finisher and even served as a stop-gap solution whenever injuries or team combinations demanded adjustment. In many ways, he has been used as India’s “spare tyre”. Someone who is always available when needed but rarely afforded the security other batters enjoy.The irony is that whenever Rahul has been handed a clearly defined role, he has thrived.Let’s take Test cricket. He was shuffled around for years until Gautam Gambhir’s management backed him as a specialist opener from the 2024-2025 Border Gavaskar Trophy. The result was immediate. With clarity came consistency; Rahul’s numbers improved significantly.But they now face a similar decision in ODI cricket. The first two ODIs against New Zealand reinforced why Rahul may be better suited to No. 5 than No. 6, especially outside the subcontinent. In Auckland, India’s middle-order wobbled after Virat Kohli’s dismissal. In Wellington, the collapse was even more pronounced as Kohli departed early and India slid to 113/7 in pursuit of just 135 before rain and DLS came to their rescue.These weren’t conditions where batters with brute force and adventures with match-ups and left-right combinations were needed. The ball seamed, there was variable bounce and prodigious movement throughout the innings. These were conditions where batters had to silence their ego and rely on an organised technique to survive and take the team home.Rahul’s value lies there. Shreyas Iyer and Rahul were India’s most convincing batters in Wellington because they could absorb pressure. Rahul’s unbeaten 26 will not feature in his CV, but it was the innings India needed most. Axar Patel , by contrast, never looked comfortable. Twice in this series he has been promoted to No. 5, and twice he has struggled to make an impact. The role made sense in India and in the Champions Trophy in UAE and the 2024 T20 World Cup, where wickets were slower, as he could hit spinners and break up a bunch of righthanders. It looks far less convincing on pitches offering assistance to fast bowlers.The numbers prove the point.Rahul has scored 1,646 runs in ODIs at No. 5 at an average of 68.58 with a strike rate exceeding 103. Axar averages 30.41 in the position. Overseas, Axar’s average falls to under 20.One understands why the team management likes the idea of Axar as a floater. It happened in the Rahul Dravid and Rohit Sharma era too. India value a left-right combination to use the unequal dimensions of certain grounds. And, with Hardik Pandya unavailable to bat at No. 6, they need batting depth till No. 8. But in trying to compensate for Hardik’s absence, are India compromising another position? If Hardik at No. 6 and Rahul at No. 5 is the World Cup blueprint, why wait until 2027 to implement it?The World Cup will be played in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, countries where early starts, fresh pitches and quality seam bowling will place the middle-order under relentless scrutiny. Their technique will trump theories.India should be using this period to give Rahul ownership of the role rather than treating him as a floating solution. Despite Axar’s whiteball skills being on the wane lately, he remains a valued asset. However, his optimum use could be lower down the order where his finishing ability and left-arm spin provide balance. Why burden him with the responsibility of rebuilding an innings in the event of a top-order collapse?Rahul has adapted to what the team needed for far too long. Perhaps it is time the team adapts to what Rahul does best.
Article Summary: Rahul has scored 1,646 runs in ODIs at No. 5 at an average of 68.58 with a strike rate exceeding 103. Axar Patel averages 30.41 in the position. Overseas, Axar’s average falls to under 20.

The WTA 250 Chennai Open women's singles final between defending champion Janice Tjen and Poland's Magda Linette has been rescheduled for Monday after rain and deteriorating air quality forced organisers to postpone Sunday's title clash at the SDAT Tennis Stadium.The championship match, which was originally scheduled to take place on Sunday, could not get underway as rain interrupted play and smoke from Diwali fireworks affected the air quality around the venue. The organisers subsequently decided to push the contest back by a day, with the final now scheduled to begin at 11 am IST on Monday, November 9.Tjen, the top seed from Indonesia, was due to face third seed Linette in a clash between two players looking to add another milestone to their Chennai Open campaigns. However, the disruption meant the tournament's closing day ended without the much-anticipated singles showdown.The decision to stage the final on Diwali had already attracted criticism, with questions being raised over the organisers' choice of date given the traditional fireworks celebrations across Chennai.The impact of the celebrations was also felt during the semi-finals, when the sound of firecrackers bursting outside the stadium repeatedly disrupted proceedings.The noise became particularly pronounced on Sunday evening as Diwali celebrations gathered pace across the city.Such disturbances are especially challenging in tennis, where players need to maintain concentration and points are generally played in silence. While spectators can cheer between points, the repeated sounds of crackers in the vicinity of the stadium made it difficult to maintain the usual playing environment.Tjen will be aiming to defend the title she won last year after securing her place in a second successive Chennai Open final. The Indonesian top seed defeated American Robin Montgomery 6-3, 6-4 in the semi-finals to move within one win of retaining her crown.Linette, meanwhile, had to fight back after dropping the opening set against seventh seed Anastasia Zakharova. The Polish player recovered to register a 2-6, 6-2, 6-3 victory and set up the final against Tjen.The third seed will be hoping to go one step further this time after finishing runner-up at the Chennai Open in 2022.Earlier on Sunday, India's Vaishnavi Adkar and Rutuja Bhosale missed out on the women's doubles title after losing to Switzerland's Simona Waltert and Naima Karamoko in straight sets.The Indian combination endured a difficult outing, going down 2-6, 0-6 as the Swiss pair controlled the match from the outset. Karamoko was particularly effective at the net, while Waltert provided dependable support from the baseline.Waltert and Karamoko secured early breaks in both sets and maintained their advantage to complete a comfortable victory and lift the doubles trophy.Despite the defeat, Adkar and Bhosale had reason to take pride in their campaign. They became the first all-Indian pairing to reach a WTA Tour-level doubles final.The Indian duo had booked their place in the championship match by producing a strong performance against second seeds Weronika Falkowska of Poland and Alana Smith of the United States. They registered a 6-2, 2-6, [10-8] victory in the semi-finals before their run ended against the Swiss combination in the final.

NEW DELHI: New Zealand have been forced into another squad reshuffle ahead of the third ODI against India, with mounting injury concerns threatening to disrupt their plans for the remainder of the series.Fast bowler Kristian Clarke has been called up as cover for Blair Tickner ahead of Tuesday's third ODI, while Lockie Ferguson has been ruled out of the fourth and fifth matches after failing to recover fully from a calf injury sustained during the T20I series.The latest developments add to New Zealand's growing list of fitness concerns, with Matt Henry also recovering from a concussion-related issue and Tickner required to undergo a mandatory stand-down period despite being cleared of concussion.Ferguson has been ruled out of the final two ODIs after failing to recover fully from a low-grade tear in his right calf. The injury was sustained during the T20I series against India.Tickner, meanwhile, was struck by a ball while batting during the second ODI. Initially cleared of concussion following his collision with Devon Conway in Auckland, the fast bowler was reassessed in Wellington and advised to target a return for the fourth ODI.New Zealand have also adjusted their plans for the transition from the ODI series to the upcoming Test assignment.Henry and Kyle Jamieson, who were initially scheduled to join the Test camp in Wellington after the third ODI, will now remain with the ODI squad for the fourth match.Two additional players are also expected to be brought into the squad across the fourth and fifth ODIs, with the composition for the final match still to be confirmed.Meanwhile, Tom Latham, Daryl Mitchell, Henry Nicholls, Glenn Phillips and Nathan Smith will leave for Wellington on Wednesday to begin preparations for the Test series. Article Title: ‘He got greedy’: Ex-India captain's blunt take on Arshdeep Singh after four-wicket haul
Article Text:

Jadeja impressed with Anshul Kamboj

Former India cricketer Ajay Jadeja has praised Arshdeep Singh's overall performance in India's five-wicket victory over New Zealand in the first ODI in Auckland, but believes the left-arm pacer could have avoided an expensive finish to his spell.India began their five-match ODI series with a comfortable win at Eden Park on Wednesday, November 4. In a rain-interrupted contest reduced to 32 overs per side, New Zealand were bowled out for 185 before India chased down the revised target of 143 in just 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli led the chase with a fluent 74, while Shubman Gill contributed 37 as the duo stitched together a 113-run partnership. India eventually crossed the finish line with five wickets to spare and 56 deliveries remaining.With the ball, Arshdeep was India's leading wicket-taker, claiming four wickets in his 10 overs. However, his figures of 4/70 were inflated by an expensive final over in which New Zealand tailender Blair Tickner struck him for three sixes, taking 23 runs off the over.Assessing the pacer's performance, Jadeja felt Arshdeep had been impressive for most of his spell but allowed the opportunity to complete a five-wicket haul to influence his bowling towards the end."I would call him slightly greedy. He himself said that as well. If you remove his last over, he had dismissed four batters before that and had given 40-odd runs. He got slightly greedy for the fifth wicket in the last over," Jadeja said on Sony Sports Network.Arshdeep had himself admitted after the match that the fifth wicket would have been his favourite, indicating that he was keen to complete a five-wicket haul. Despite missing out on the milestone, his four-wicket effort placed him in an exclusive group of Indian fast bowlers to achieve the feat in an ODI in New Zealand, alongside Javagal Srinath and Mohammed Shami.Jadeja, however, stressed that the expensive final over should not overshadow what Arshdeep brings to India's bowling combination. He pointed to the value of having a left-arm fast bowler in an attack that already features Jasprit Bumrah, adding that the competition for places would only benefit the team."It happens. It's natural, but Arshdeep Singh is showing that he can play in ODIs as well, which I believe is a very good thing when a left-arm seamer gets added to this attack with (Jasprit) Bumrah. The competition has increased a lot, which is very good for India," Jadeja elaborated.Jadeja also reserved praise for Anshul Kamboj, who delivered an economical spell of 2/22 from his 10 overs and walked away with the Player of the Match award.The former India batter acknowledged that Kamboj had faced questions over his bowling during his Test debut against England in 2025, particularly regarding his pace and tendency to bowl no-balls. However, he felt the youngster had shown considerable improvement in Auckland.Jadeja also suggested that Kamboj's workload before the England assignment could have contributed to his struggles, pointing out that fatigue can affect a bowler's execution. His performance against New Zealand, according to Jadeja, reflected better pace, consistency and accuracy."He bowled extremely well. The vision everyone had was that he didn't have pace when he played in England and was bowling a lot of no-balls. I think he had come after playing a lot of cricket then. So a guy also gets tired. It's not that easy. Then he was playing for the first time, but the consistency and the slight increase in his pace he showed today (Wednesday), if we talk about the accuracy amongst the four bowlers, it's Anshul Kamboj," Jadeja added.
Article Summary: India beat New Zealand by five wickets in the first ODI in Auckland. Ajay Jadeja praised Arshdeep Singh's performance, but said he could have avoided expensive final over. Jadeja also praised Anshul Kamboj's bowling, saying he had shown improvement.

Check.Easier said than done, but the stability and fluency he has brought to the batting line-up speak volumes about his character and strong mindset. Rahul has excelled in whatever situation the team has demanded of him. There have been numerous instances when he has played the role of an accelerator, accumulator or rebuilder, and not once has he looked out of place. More importantly, he has never looked out of his depth.For someone who opens in Test cricket, adjusting to batting lower down the order in ODIs is more than a subtle change. But Rahul has used different methods to avoid the madness. At the Dubai nets during the 2025 Champions Trophy, the focus was on teeing off from ball one against the old ball.Meanwhile, in New Zealand, the emphasis has been on ensuring a tight set-up and getting enough repetitions in to trigger muscle memory.Sitanshu Kotak, who has overseen countless net sessions, is not surprised that Rahul rarely appears under pressure in clutch situations."I think Rahul's biggest advantage is that he is opening in red-ball. Sometimes he goes at No. 5 in ODIs - his record is so good there - and he is so good at No. 6 also. So he plays according to the need of the team. And since I have joined, I can't remember many matches where he got batting and he has not contributed. He has played some unbelievable innings and under pressure, he never looks under pressure," said Kotak at the pre-match press conference."I have never seen KL under pressure, so you always see him very stable and most of the time he has never let the team down, so that is brilliant to have someone like him who has that experience. That temperament and that game also. Someone who can rotate, who can hit boundaries when required. He can easily hit a few sixes, so that is a great thing to have someone like KL," added Kotak.Even while preparing for different roles and situations, Rahul rarely gives the impression that he is doing anything different. The designated No. 5 for India during the 2023 ODI World Cup faced a lot of flak for his knock in the title clash, which unfairly overshadowed his contributions earlier in the tournament, including the tone-setting 97 against Australia in Chennai.Rahul walked in with the scoreboard reading 2/3 during the 200-run chase and helped push the team over the line in the tournament's opening match.A similar situation unfolded in the second ODI in Wellington when a top-order collapse reduced India to 39/3. However, the team management persisted with Axar Patel at No. 5, keeping Rahul at No. 6. He has been batting in that position for quite some time, and the second ODI was another reminder of his all-weather skills in the format.The sample size was not big enough to grab headlines, but the unbeaten 26 off 38 balls had class written all over it. Rahul battled Kyle Jamieson and Jacob Duffy with authority. There was awkward bounce and enough seam movement to keep batters from both teams on their toes, but Rahul remained unflinching.The ease with which he dealt with chin music would have provided another layer of assurance to the dressing room about his ability to handle whatever comes their way in the build-up to the next fifty-over extravaganza and the tournament itself.With the conditions in South Africa in mind, there is strong chatter about promoting the wicketkeeper-batter back to No. 5. While this may seem like a change to the outside world, it is just a number for Rahul.The conditions, situation and batting position may change, but the rock holding India's middle order together will remain the same.
Article Summary: KL Rahul has transformed into a middle-order rock in India's ODI set-up. The wicketkeeper-batter has been doing the heavy lifting for the side. Rahul has excelled in whatever situation the team has demanded of him.

Article Title: 'Everyone knows how to play on a green wicket': Kusal Mendis backs Sri Lanka batters to tackle Pakistan's pace challenge
Article Text:
Sri Lanka's captain Kusal Mendis (AP Photo)

First Test assignment as captain for Kusal Mendis

Mendis backs experienced bowling attack to deliver

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mendis praises Pakistan's hospitality and security arrangements

Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis is confident his experienced batting line-up has the technique and temperament to counter Pakistan's expected pace-friendly conditions as the visitors prepare for the opening Test in Rawalpindi on Monday. With the hosts potentially opting for a greener surface to bring their fast bowlers into the contest, Mendis has backed his senior batters to rise to the challenge, insisting their experience of playing in England will hold them in good stead.The Sri Lankan skipper believes the presence of experienced campaigners such as Dinesh Chandimal and Dhananjaya de Silva, alongside himself, gives the team the necessary confidence to negotiate challenging conditions away from home."We know they will be giving a little bit different wicket. I think the batters have to manage our skills and preparation well. I know we have a very good batting line-up with some very senior players... Dinesh Chandimal, Dhananjaya de Silva, myself, and a couple of other guys."Everyone knows how to play on a green wicket. We played really well in England also, so I have no doubt in my batting line-up," Mendis told reporters.The Rawalpindi Test will mark Mendis' first assignment as Sri Lanka's Test captain after he took over the leadership from Dhananjaya de Silva in early October. The 31-year-old admitted that leading the side in the longest format was something he was particularly looking forward to, despite the challenges of an extended stay in Pakistan.Sri Lanka have spent more than a month in the country, having arrived for the preceding white-ball assignments. Mendis acknowledged that spending such a long period away from home, largely between hotels and training sessions, had not been easy for the players.However, he said the squad had found ways to keep itself occupied and was now fully focused on switching gears for Test cricket."Honestly, compared to ODIs and T20s, Test cricket is very different. I think everyone mostly likes to play Test cricket. Me as well. I'm very happy to captain in Test cricket," he said."It's not easy, sometimes we stay in the hotel and come to practice and that's it... I think it's a little bit hard to stay one month in a hotel. But we do some stuff in the team room, games and individual things to keep ourselves entertained."Sri Lanka are yet to register a Test victory in their two series this year against West Indies and India, but Mendis believes the performances of his bowling unit offer plenty of encouragement ahead of the Pakistan challenge.The skipper pointed to the experience within the attack, highlighting how the fast bowlers have delivered consistently across formats and are equipped to handle the demands of Test cricket.Sri Lanka have several pace options at their disposal, with Asitha Fernando, Lahiru Kumara, Dilshan Madushanka and Eshan Malinga forming the fast-bowling contingent alongside all-rounder Milan Rathnayake. Left-arm spinner Prabath Jayasuriya will lead the spin department."We have a very balanced side, both with the bowling and batting unit. I think we've done really well in the past couple of tours in the bowling side, and same in one-day cricket. The fast-bowling attack is doing well," Mendis said."We have a very senior bowling unit, the guys have played so many first-class and international matches. Same in the batting, so everyone is ready for tomorrow's game."Beyond preparations for the series, Mendis also expressed satisfaction with the arrangements made by the Pakistan Cricket Board during Sri Lanka's extended stay in the country.The Sri Lankan captain praised the security arrangements and said the players had been comfortable with the local food, which he felt was similar to the cuisine back home."Security-wise, everybody is very happy. Food, we normally eat spicy and everything, so same like in Sri Lanka it's in Pakistan. I think everyone has had a happy stay in Pakistan," he added.
Article Summary: Kusal Mendis confident Sri Lanka's experienced batting line-up has the technique and temperament to counter Pakistan's expected pace-friendly conditions. Sri Lanka face Pakistan in the first Test in Rawalpindi on Monday. The 31-year-old says he is looking forward to leading the side in the longest format.

Article Title: 'We were 20-30 runs short': India U19 captain Lakshya Raichandani on defeat against Pakistan
Article Text:
India Captain Lakshya Raichandani (Image: IANS)

'We were 20-30 runs short': Raichandani admits India's batting failure

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Raichandani admits India could have bowled better

India Under-19 captain Lakshya Raichandani admitted his side failed to put up a competitive total after Pakistan pulled off a remarkable three-wicket victory in their ACC Men's U19 Asia Cup Group A clash in Oman on Sunday. Despite Arjun Rajput's fighting century, India could not capitalise on a promising recovery, allowing Pakistan to chase down 209 with 11 balls to spare.Pakistan were in serious trouble at 61/5 before Hamza Zahoor produced a match-winning unbeaten 100 off 108 deliveries. His composed knock, supported by Hasnain Abbas Dar's valuable 38, turned the contest around and handed Pakistan their second consecutive victory in the tournament.Speaking after the match, Raichandani acknowledged that India were at least 20-30 runs below a competitive total and rued the lack of partnerships around Rajput's innings.India, who elected to bat after winning the toss, suffered an early collapse and were reduced to 42/4. Rajput then took charge with a magnificent 107, keeping India's innings together and helping them recover from a difficult position.However, the Indian captain felt the team could have added significantly more runs had another batter stayed with Rajput for longer."Yeah, they weren't enough. We were 20-30 runs short, but overall there were some good innings from Arjun and a good contribution from KP (Kavya Patel). It was a really good innings, and if someone had stayed there with him (Arjun), it could have been a little bit more total," Raichandani said during the post-match presentation.India eventually folded for 208 in 46.3 overs, leaving their bowlers with a target that Pakistan managed to overhaul despite losing five wickets early in the chase.The India skipper also conceded that his bowlers missed opportunities to finish the job after putting Pakistan under considerable pressure. Pakistan were struggling at 61/5, but Zahoor and Dar combined to rebuild the innings and shift the momentum in their team's favour. Raichandani felt India could have been more clinical during that phase."Yeah, definitely. We will try to rectify it, and there was a lot of positive from this game. We will try to take that forward. There were some really good efforts. They were 60 for 5. We could have bowled a little bit better, but overall, it was really good," he added.
Article Summary: Pakistan beat India by three wickets in ACC Men's U19 Asia Cup Group A clash in Oman on Sunday. India captain Lakshya Raichandani admits his side were 20-30 runs short of a competitive total. India eventually folded for 208 in 46.3 overs, leaving their bowlers with a target of 209.
